sections.title: Neural networks, 1943–1986 · a static vector and a few categories
teaching: The vowel network returns as a summary of what neural networks could do in their first period, from **1943 to 1986**. Two formants come in, weighted connections pass them through three hidden layers, and five outputs give a response for done, dune, dean, Don and Dan. The weights are the same illustrative signed weights used for forward propagation and backpropagation.

The two ends of that period are marked by sources on the page. On the left is **McCulloch and Pitts (1943)**, “A Logical Calculus of the Ideas Immanent in Nervous Activity.” Its abstract starts from the **“all-or-none” character of nervous activity** and treats neural events with propositional logic, the idea that a neuron either fires or does not. On the right are the two **Parallel Distributed Processing** volumes from 1986, the books that brought networks of many simple connected units, trained by adjusting weights, into wide use.

The caption states what such a network could do. **Given some static vector of formants, the NN could make a decision about a few possible categories.** A static vector is one fixed list of numbers, here F1 and F2, measured at a single moment. The network takes that one input and picks among five words. The caption also states the limit. **Human cognition is far more complex.** Speech unfolds in time, a sentence is a long sequence of words, and what comes next depends on what came before. A network that maps one fixed vector to a handful of labels has no way to represent a sequence or to keep track of earlier inputs.

To handle language, a network has to take in many vectors in order and use the earlier ones when it responds to the later ones. That requirement is what separates these classifiers from recurrent networks and, later, large language models.

sections.title: Jordan’s recurrent network for speech production
teaching: In **1985, Michael Jordan developed recurrent neural networks** to make sense of **speech production**. The page traces a line from that work to **LLMs** and then to **agentic AI**. The photo on the right is Michael Jordan.

The network diagram has four kinds of units. **Plan units** receive input from outside and say which sequence to produce. **Hidden units** combine information, and **output units** produce the network’s response. The new part is the **state units**. The outputs loop back along the long curved arrows into the state units, and each state unit also feeds back to itself.

Those loops are what make the network **recurrent**. At each moment the state units hold a trace of what the network has just produced, and that trace feeds into the hidden units together with the plan. The next output therefore depends on the plan and on the network’s own recent outputs. A feedforward classifier has no such memory, because each input passes straight through once. The plot, **Performance on /istrstry/**, shows the network producing a sequence of sounds over time, from 0 to 32 time steps. Each row is one articulatory feature, **Voice, Place, Sonorant, Sibilant, Nasal, Height, Back and Round**, and each line gives how much of that feature the output has at each moment. Sibilant rises in bumps where the s sounds occur, while Nasal and Height stay nearly flat.

The **Round** line rises early and stays high for most of the sequence instead of switching on and off for single sounds. A feature spreads across neighboring sounds because the network’s outputs blend from one moment to the next. Producing a smooth, overlapping sequence like this is what a recurrent network adds to speech, and the same idea of feeding past outputs back in runs through to today’s language models.
concepts: plan, state, hidden and output units

sections.title: From one neuron to agentic systems
teaching: The page builds up in four steps, from one neuron to a full agentic system, and then names the two operations underneath all of them. The first column is **one neuron**. A vector **x** comes in, each part is multiplied by a weight **w**, and the neuron sums them to give one number **y**. **Vector in, one number out.** That sum is an inner product.

The second column is a **network**. Here the layers are 4, 3, 4 and 5 units, joined by weight sets **W₁, W₂ and W₃**. Each W turns one vector into the next vector, and the last layer is a **decision vector**, one value per possible answer. **Vector in, decision vector out.** This is the kind of network used for the vowels.

The third column is an **LLM**. Now **vectors 1 through 15** go in at the bottom, one per token, and pass up through **5 layers** of W blocks. The six colors of W stand for six different kinds of weight sets. At the top, the model produces **vector 16**, drawn as a small bar chart labeled **PDF**, a probability distribution over what the next token will be. The LLM is described as **a dynamical system with many vectors in and one decision vector out**. The fourth column is an **agentic system, a graph of LLMs**. Separate LLMs are connected in order, **Outline, Write, Critic, Revise and Final**, with a **loop** between Critic and Revise. One model drafts, another critiques, another revises, and the critique can send the work back for more revision before the final model finishes. The parts are LLMs, and the system is the way they are wired together.

Under all four, the bottom line names what they share. **Inference is inner products**, weighted sums passed from layer to layer, whether in one neuron or in a large model. **Learning is SGD plus DP**, stochastic gradient descent guided by the dynamic-programming bookkeeping of backpropagation. The same two operations scale from the vowel classifier to an LLM.
concepts: agentic graph with a critic loop

sections.title: Fifteen vectors · the same next-item question for any sequence
teaching: The page starts with **15 vectors, x₁ to x₁₅**, and an empty slot for **x₁₆**, and asks **vectors of what?** An LLM receives a sequence of vectors and predicts the next one. The four reveals show four different kinds of sequence fed into the same arrangement.

First, a **sentence cut into 15 words**. “The cat that the dog chased ran up the old tree and sat on the ___.” Each vector stands for one word, and **x₁₆ is the missing word**. Predicting it requires using words far back in the sentence, since it is the cat that sat on something.

Next, the words disappear and a **spectrogram is cut into 15 frames**, from 0 to 5 kHz along the vertical axis with time running to the right. Each vector is now one slice of sound, and **x₁₆ is the next frame**. Then an **image of a house, a tree and the sun is cut into 16 patches**, read row by row. Fifteen patches are vectors, and **x₁₆ is the missing bottom-right patch**. The last example is a **protein, the insulin B chain**, read as **15 amino acids**, F V N Q H L C G S H L V E A L, drawn folding into a helix. Each amino acid is a vector, and **x₁₆ is the next residue**, which is **Y**. The same sixteenth slot sits at the end of every sequence.

The takeaway states the point of the four examples. **The LLM only ever sees vectors.** Words, sounds, pixels and molecules all become sequences of vectors, so **one machine asks one question, what is x₁₆?** Whatever the source, learning to predict the next vector in a sequence is the task the model is built for.

sections.title: Which sequences can be English words?
teaching: The page asks which strings of sounds can be English words, building the answer in three rows. The first row has twenty **one-syllable words with a single consonant, a single vowel and a single consonant**, such as Don, mat, sit, cup, fish and ring. Consonants are dark, vowels red, and a silent e grey. The rule for this row is that **a simple syllable in English can have a consonant, then a vowel, then a consonant**.

The second row adds **clusters**, groups of consonants. Real words with clusters before the vowel, called **onsets**, include split, flat, black, glad and stop. Real words with clusters after the vowel, called **codas**, include desk, box, help, milk and lamp. Each real word has an **impossible twin** below it, marked with a star, such as *sblit, *lfat, *bnack, *dlad and *tsop, and *desb, *bokp, *hepl, *mikl and *lapm.

Many twins use the same letters in the opposite order, flat and *lfat, help and *hepl, lamp and *lapm. **Order matters**, and the pattern mirrors around the vowel. An onset like fl is fine, but the same sounds reversed as lf cannot start a word, although the reversed order can end a word. The rule for this row is that **only certain sequences are allowed before the vowel and after the vowel**. The third row has **words of many syllables**, with dots marking syllable breaks, such as **ba·na·na, win·dow, pump·kin, nap·kin, At·lan·tic, ath·lete, ad·mit and spa·ghet·ti**. Atlantic, athlete and admit contain t followed by l, th followed by l, and d followed by m. Those pairs are fine inside the word because a syllable break falls between them, but they cannot begin a word, so *tlantic, *thlete and *dmit are impossible. Likewise ng can end a syllable, as in ring, but never start one, so *ngapkin is impossible.

The rule for the whole page is that **a long word is a chain of syllables**, and every syllable obeys the same rules. **t·l is fine across a break, but tl cannot start a syllable.** This is **phonotactic knowledge**, the knowledge of which sound sequences a language allows, and English speakers have it without ever being taught it.

sections.title: Guessing the next letter reveals phonotactic knowledge
teaching: The pop quiz asks how **phonotactic knowledge can be revealed through GPT learning**. Each item is the start of an English word, and the task is to **guess the next letter**. The nine starts are ra_, sp_, k_, skr_, m_, bram_, b_, f_ and sh_. People agree quickly on most of them, and how much they agree changes from item to item.

After **ra_**, likely letters include t, n, r and l. **After a vowel, almost anything** can follow, so the guesses spread out. After **sp_**, the next letter is **l, r or a vowel**, and *spn is never possible. After **k_**, a vowel or **n**, as in knee, and never *kt. After **b_** and **f_**, the choices are **r, l or a vowel**, never *bn or *fn. After **sh_**, a vowel or **r**, as in shrimp, never *shb.

Some starts narrow the choices even more. After **skr_** only a vowel can come next, never *skrl, and after **m_** at the start of a word only a vowel, never *mb. After **bram_**, the letter b is almost forced, as in bramble, though a new syllable could also start there. At the start of a word the choices shrink sharply, while after a vowel they open up again. These guesses follow the rules for English syllables. What can follow a starting consonant is exactly what an English onset allows, and the impossible continuations are clusters that English never allows at the start of a syllable. Guessing well requires knowing English phonotactics.

The takeaway connects this to LLMs. **Guessing the next letter is predicting x₁₆.** A **GPT trained only on this game learns English sounds and spelling**, because its predicted distribution has to match these patterns. After fa_ its distribution is spread flat over many letters, and after skr_ it is sharply peaked on a few vowels.
